title: Movement of Substances
seo_title: Secondary 3 Biology: Movement of Substances Worksheets (O-Level 6093 with Answers)
standard_text: Define diffusion and describe its importance to living organisms; define osmosis in terms of water potential and a partially permeable membrane and describe the effects of solutions of different water potentials on plant and animal cells; define active transport and describe its importance, such as the uptake of mineral ions by root hair cells; relate surface area to volume ratio to the rate of diffusion (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Biology 6093 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Biology worksheets on movement of substances: diffusion, osmosis, water potential, active transport, potato strip experiments and surface area to volume ratio. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Water moves from high to low water potential.
key_sub: Active transport goes against the gradient and needs energy.
body_html:
How to think about it

Three ways substances move in and out of cells.

  • Diffusion: net movement from higher to lower concentration. No energy.
  • Osmosis: water moves from higher to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane. Pure water has the highest water potential.
  • Active transport: against the concentration gradient, using energy from respiration.
  • Percentage change in mass = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100. Smaller objects have a larger surface area to volume ratio.
Example

4.00 g potato becomes 3.60 g. % change?

(3.60 − 4.00) ÷ 4.00 × 100

Answer: −10%

Example

Red blood cell in pure water?

water enters by osmosis

no cell wall

Answer: swells and bursts

Common mistakes

  • Saying water moves to a higher water potential.
  • Calling osmosis the movement of solute.
  • Saying plant cells burst in pure water.
  • Dividing by the final mass in percentage change.

faq.q: What is the difference between diffusion and osmosis?
faq.a: Diffusion is the net movement of any particles down a concentration gradient. Osmosis is only the movement of water, from a higher to a lower water potential, through a partially permeable membrane.

faq.q: What happens to plant cells in a concentrated solution?
faq.a: Water leaves by osmosis, the vacuole shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall: the cell is plasmolysed.

faq.q: Why does active transport need energy?
faq.a: It moves particles against their concentration gradient, so energy from respiration is needed.

items.q: Why does active transport need energy?
c: It moves substances down a gradient.
It happens only in dead cells.
It moves substances against a concentration gradient.
items.e: Energy comes from respiration in mitochondria.

items.q: Glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into the blood against a concentration gradient. Which process is this?
items.e: Diffusion: particles from high to low concentration. Osmosis: water through a partially permeable membrane. Active transport: against the gradient, using energy.

items.q: Why is turgidity important to a plant?
c: It lets the plant absorb sugar.
